items.title: Trump is Coming for your Credit Card Rewards. That’s good. (Vox, Eric Levitz)
items.text:
Apparently more people thinking about these things right now.

Saw *this* in the morning (*it's like the algos are spying on me!*)

https://x.com/ThomasEWoods/status/2112522999480078678

I almost never say this... but **Tom Woods is straight-up, downright, 100% WRONG here**

> Wall Street is sending the public a dire warning: President Donald Trump has become a threat to the very foundation of American freedom — your frequent flier miles. Okay, America’s big banks haven’t been using rhetoric *quite* that grandiose. But they are accusing Trump of **imperiling Americans’ credit card rewards.**

Yes, America shouldn't *have* credit card rewards. They're a dumb, intransparent, rent-seeking, unfair redistribution mechanism https://stacker.news/items/1598123, https://stacker.news/items/1598593. Yes, I know it's a lefty talking point... but you can hate the loyalty ~~schemes~~ scams *without* a bleeding-heart consideration for the poor.

***

> This affordability gain does come at a cost; American cardholders do tend to reap higher rewards than Australian or European ones. But **this is not a good trade from the standpoint of economic justice; few think it is fair to take money from the poor to give to the rich.**

![](https://m.stacker.news/162315)

not weighing into the political drama of this, or whether or not this specific government legislation (which I know nothing about) is a good/useful way to improve the world...

## ..."working tirelessly to pass the Credit Card Competition Act, in order to stop the out of control Swipe Fee ripoff!”

At least the president is right about the **"out of control \[sic!] Swipe Fee \[sic!] ripoff"**

> Large retailers are lobbying hard to get the Credit Card Competition Act passed during December’s lame-duck congressional session. Banks have responded by issuing a “code red,” in the words of the Wall Street Journal. In recent days, their lobbyists have warned policymakers that, if swipe fees fall, credit cardholders’ cash rewards and travel points will go down with them.

Yeah, that two major industries are at clear, incentive-based cross-purposes here should tell you something about the insane situation in the first place... *what the banking/loyalty/points scheme gains, the retailers lose*. Your rewards come out of businesses' interchange fees in the first place (and secondly, if you play the game well, at the expense of unsophisticated/naive customers elsewhere, like we discussed yesterday https://stacker.news/items/1598123)

## "*if* the banks’ big-picture story is right — and the law cuts both swipe fees and credit card rewards — that would probably *benefit* the average American."

Precisely.

***

## "we need to first examine how the credit card system currently works — and whom it does and doesn’t benefit."

Alright, cool; that's what we came for:

> Whenever you use a credit card to purchase a banana from Aldi, or volleyball from Dick’s, or an adult-sized Grape Fanta Can Halloween costume from Party City, the retailer must pay a fee to the bank that issued your card. The bank then uses that revenue to fund your rewards.

> Critically, merchants don’t just eat the costs of swipe fees. Rather, they [pass on part](https://archive.md/o/RqIwZ/https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/research-department-working-paper/2020/distributional-effects-payment-card-pricing-merchant-cost-pass-through-united-states-canada.aspx) of the expense to consumers, in the form of higher prices. Some businesses concentrate these price hikes on card users (for example, barbershops often charge less if you pay with cash). But most retailers charge every customer the same price, regardless of their payment method.

Yup, we know.

> shoppers who pay with cash or debit effectively subsidize those who pay with cards: The former face higher prices than they would in a world without credit cards, yet they receive no “cash back” or travel points in recompense.

I repeat the graph from yesterday: (authors used FICO scores to proxy well-off, but you can just think of what the graph reflects in reality as outsider-insider or the x-axis showing how *well* you play the loyalty scam game.) YES, if you play well, you can eke out some benefits... but most people, most of the time *lose out*. 

![](https://m.stacker.news/162348)

> This arrangement seems unfair on its face. But it is especially troubling when one considers class disparities in the use of credit cards and receipt of rewards.

> As a general rule, the higher a person’s income, the more they use credit cards. In 2024, US households who earned less than $25,000 a year put just [17 percent](https://archive.md/o/RqIwZ/https://www.frbservices.org/wp-content/uploads/2025-diary-of-consumer-payment-choice.pdf%23page=13) of their payments on credit cards; among households earning more than $150,000, that figure was 51 percent, according to Federal Reserve data.

...and higher income basically proxy ~higher FICOs so yeah: **What you're saying is those better off play this game more; yes, exactly.**

It's not (like the author focuses on and what turns our friend Tom Woods off) primarily wrong that the poor are getting screwed. They *are*, but we (mostly) don't care about that (fuck the boomers, who are rich; but also, fuck the poor.) 

It's because loyalty programs are *intransparent, unnecessary,* [centralizing](https://stacker.news/items/1598593)*,* and faces the rich with incentives to play useless, low-paid games -- *or* face high enough opportunity cost that optimizing become prohibitively expensive; **thus constituting a wealth transfer *to the financial industry*** (and the portion of major companies, GE or airlines/hotels or Starbucks, that have *turned into* proto-banks https://stacker.news/items/743123).

oh, *sweet*:

> According to a [2026 working paper](https://archive.md/o/RqIwZ/https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w35067/w35067.pdf) from the National Bureau of Economic Research, the credit card system takes, on average, **$88 a year from households** with annual incomes below $150,000, while delivering an average yearly benefit of **$390 to households** with incomes above that threshold.

Credit cards...

> serve a variety of valuable economic purposes, from helping households weather unexpected expenses and irregular incomes to facilitating online commerce. And maintaining a credit card system costs money: Banks need to finance the loans they extend, while payment networks must maintain vast computer systems to process transactions and detect fraud.

Yeah, I mean, they *don't*: we have a better monetary system that doesn't require that (but admittedly, requires *other* expenses https://stacker.news/items/1598748)

## "Yet America’s credit card system is needlessly expensive. Our nation’s merchants — and thus, consumers — pay far higher swipe fees than their counterparts in other rich countries."

THIS comparison I'm less sold on: $100 spent in...

* **America** (standard visa vs premium): cost merchant 1.23-2.07
* **Canada**: $0.95
* **EU and Australia**: capped at $0.30 (though, usually with high/higher fixed fees or machine rents or annual sign-up fees)

OK, *now* we're back to the usual government-botching-things and stop regulating stupid shit:

> Under the CCCA, however, Party City would be able to accept Visa on a transaction — without necessarily *using* Visa to process the payment. Instead, the bank that issued the customer’s Visa would need to provide Party City with at least one alternative payment processor — a different network that has no relationship with Visa and which might offer lower fees. The law’s authors hope — and the banking industry fears — that this mandatory competition will force down swipe fees. But **it’s not clear how much of a difference the CCCA would actually make.**

JUST red tape in a separate form. Fuck it. 

***

TL;DR, the article and its author is *completely* right but for *accidental/entirely wrong* reasons. It's not the welfare of the poor (or redistribution) that's wrong, it's a secondary (tertiary?) monetary system, with intransparent non-par prices, nudging everyone to play a heavily skewed, mostly negative-sum game.

## JUST. DON'T.

items.title: The Great Dilution
items.text:
In a 1974 cable released by Wikileaks, primary dealers explicitly planned to use gold futures volatility to "diminish initial demand for physical holding and negate long-term hoarding by US citizens." Furthermore, these primary dealers were of the opinion that U.S. citizens, on the whole, weren't psychologically prepared to switch from small scale gold purchases to large scale, long term bullion hoarding except maybe for gold coins. To put things in context, this was just after it was now legal again for American citizens to own physical gold and the predictions of the primary dealers turned out to be true. As of today, paper trading of gold surpasses physical demand for gold and is 200 times larger than the latter. 

Gold is hard to move and slow to settle, so the world delegated its custody to banks, which issued paper claims against it. Those claims could be multiplied well beyond the metal behind them. Today, unallocated accounts in the London bullion market give holders a claim on a pool of metal, not title to a particular bar. Gold was never outlawed again but It was diluted when its price discovery moved to paper.
 
The Iceberg


The point of this brief walk down memory lane is to serve as a reminder that in times of economic crisis it’s always the unsuspecting public that is psyoped into paying the consequences whilst the architects get fat government handouts. With sovereign debt levels far exceeding global GDP, inflation raging, high energy prices thanks in part to the conflict in Iran, an out of control money printer and a higher unemployment rate; it would be a gross understatement to say that an economic iceberg is on the horizon. 

Bitcoin: Protest Money


Understanding these historical precedents is important in the era of Bitcoin because the same forces that converged to neuter gold after WW I and more so in the 1970s are much bigger today and have already been unleashed on the Bitcoin ecosystem over the years. Bitcoin emerged as protest money against the abuse of trust by monetary institutions that have been custodians of the financial system for centuries. 

As an asset without an issuer, Bitcoin doesn’t have counterparty risk that comes with trusted third parties and it’s more than just a store of value asset as most Wall Street pundits and the media lapdogs would have you believe. As an alternative monetary system, it exists to enable you to transact permissionlessly and ultimately be the bedrock of a new financial system. Bitcoin, is therefore, more than a store of value but It’s a monetary system designed to eliminate the need for trusted third parties. Thus, reducing it to a Wall Street investment product misses the point because even if Bitcoin  appreciates in price but is increasingly held through intermediaries, it can succeed as a financial asset while failing, for many holders, as an instrument of monetary sovereignty; and this is why the attack on self-custody becomes important. You cannot easily confiscate a decentralised monetary network by shutting down a central issuer that does not exist but you can pressure its users to surrender control of their coins.

Every previous promise of trusted custody in the Bitcoin ecosystem has ended in betrayal. Mt. Gox in 2014 lost 850,000 coins, roughly seven percent of all Bitcoin in circulation at the time, to a theft the exchange concealed for years. Celsius, BlockFi, and Voyager sold themselves as the safe, regulated option and went bankrupt in 2022 with customer funds re-hypothecated into illiquid, sometimes unsecured loans. FTX, which was the second-largest exchange at the time, with celebrity advisors and investors, endorsed by regulators, audited by Tier-1 firms; vapourized eight billion dollars of customer deposits in a single weekend through a backdoor that funneled balances to a trading firm also owned by Sam Bankman-Fried. In every case the customer believed he held Bitcoin or its dollar equivalent; but in reality what he held was an IOU, which wasn’t as liquid as people thought.



The Seven-Step Playbook


The case against self-custody can be classified into seven steps
Unmask users and destroy privacy. France’s finance committee voted for a declaration on self-custody wallets above €100,000, exempting custodian-held coins.
Make it very inconvenient. Since 2024, EU rules require exchanges to verify wallet ownership above €1,000.
Target developers. The Samourai Wallet developer received five years for software that never held user funds, which sends a chilling signal to anyone building privacy tools.
Make it intimidating. Reported firmware flaws and drained hardware wallets teach users that self-custody is risky.
Let the lists leak. Bribed Coinbase staff exposed tens of thousands of customers’ details, and France’s tax office was breached. Databases of holders become target lists.
Make it dangerous. Wrench attacks and home invasions are rising.
Offer the safe option. BlackRock cut its ETF conversion minimum from $25 million to $1 million, citing “kidnappings, ransom, custody failures.” The underlying coins sit with a custodian.

This pitch is identical to the one used to herd gold buyers into unallocated LBMA accounts half a century ago; keep your metal with us, the vault is safer than your house, and besides, the price is the same.  A self-custodied coin is base money; an ETF share is a credit instrument whose value collapses exactly when its issuer or custodian fails; which is to say, exactly when you most need it. The ETF, like the futures contract before it, makes Bitcoin legible to legacy balance sheets precisely by removing the property; direct settlement without counterparty, that made it a settlement network in the first place. In short, you no longer hold your keys but you are holding a position in a Bitcoin financial product, and the difference between those two states is the difference between sovereignty and a margin call. 

The Margin Call Trap


When these mechanisms from the debt=based fiat system are ported onto a sound money base, more and more people are separated from their coins. It works like this; 
The custodian holds your coin
You borrow dollars against it
You spend the dollars
The custodian now owns the collateral and the loan, and you own the obligation. 

When the price rises the arrangement feels like wealth, with everyone feeling like a genius. However, when the price falls the custodian issues a margin call you cannot meet without selling or topping up your balance with more Bitcoin, at the price the custodian's own desk has just helped establish. This is the 1974 unallocated-account pattern with one improvement, where instead of asking you to surrender gold in exchange for a paper claim, the complex now asks you to surrender Bitcoin in exchange for the “privilege” of going into debt against it. Fractional-reserve banking is fraud because the bank promises redemption to every depositor while lending the same funds to multiple borrowers. The Bitcoin-custody-plus-loan product recreates the fraud at the asset level, with one deposit and one borrower; both you.

Ownership Is Not Control


Owning an asset is not the same as controlling it. You can own an ETF that tracks Bitcoin’s price, leave your coins on an exchange, or pledge them to a lender and still participate in the Bitcoin market; but none of these arrangements gives you the same monetary sovereignty as holding your own keys and retaining the ability to authorize your own transactions. Self-custody is how an individual exercises that freedom. 

The Price of Freedom


None of this means self-custody is without risk. You become responsible for securing your keys, protecting your backups, planning for inheritance, and ensuring that you can recover access when something goes wrong. These responsibilities demand education, preparation, and discipline. That said, there is a fundamental difference between accepting responsibility for your own money and outsourcing that responsibility to an institution whose interests may not always align with yours. The choice, therefore, is not between risk and safety. It is between different kinds of risk, different forms of responsibility, and different degrees of control. Above all, do not confuse the convenience of a financial product with the freedom of owning money you can control yourself.

The Final Word


The financial-industrial complex does not need to destroy Bitcoin to neutralize its promise. It only needs to convince enough people that exercising that freedom is too inconvenient, too frightening, or too dangerous to be worth the effort. It needs you to surrender control voluntarily, until a monetary system designed to eliminate the need for trusted intermediaries becomes just another asset class dependent on them.
Do not mistake the surrender of responsibility for the achievement of safety. Do not mistake exposure to Bitcoin’s price for possession of Bitcoin itself. Above all, never forget that the freedom Bitcoin offers is not something a custodian can exercise on your behalf.

items.title: The Gospel according to Peter (Thiel) - We have Peter Thiel’s secret lectures
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/162413)

> It’s a time of apocalyptic worldviews in Silicon Valley. The latest AI doom cycle is driven by effective altruism (EA), a philosophy that has lurked around the fringes for years but recently burst into the mainstream because its adherents are embedded across the AI industry, from Anthropic to newly appointed AI safety watchdog METR. EA is a utilitarian approach to charity premised on doing the most good for the most people over the longest time, and EA advocates see [halting an AI-induced doomsday](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/hGwAohPbwCrDT5ynY/ea-as-antichrist-understanding-peter-thiel) as critical to saving as many humans as possible.

> But EA has an important and equally apocalyptic rival in the crosscutting cosmologies of the tech titans — a strain of Christianity best represented by Peter Thiel, who believes EA will [bring about the Antichrist](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/hGwAohPbwCrDT5ynY/ea-as-antichrist-understanding-peter-thiel). It’s an issue on which the billionaire techno-capitalist is a self-styled expert, and, somehow, Thiel has become America’s most provocative and visible Christian theologian.

> Thiel’s current fixation on the End of the World as We Know It is in theological language called eschatology, the study of the “last things.” His specific bête noire is the Antichrist, the villain of these end times scenarios. Thiel’s riffs on the Antichrist began a little over three years ago, first in [a 2023 talk](https://wisdomofcrowds.live/p/the-temptation-of-peter-thiel) at the Catholic University of America but then, starting in 2025, only in closed-door, invitation-only, multipart lectures out of San Francisco. While that secrecy is frustrating for those of us interested in how uber-rich and politically powerful tech titans see the future of our world, it’s also rather savvy — no surprise from the guy who started hugely successful ventures like PayPal and Palantir. “It’s a pretty good marketing shtick if you want everybody to hear about something, not to let anybody in the room,” Thiel [reportedly](https://observer.co.uk/news/international/article/tech-billionaire-thiel-claims-regulators-are-the-antichrist) told one San Francisco audience last fall. In March, he traveled to Rome for another private, four-part series on the Antichrist. Taking his shtick to the doorstep of the Vatican was guaranteed to generate publicity, [and it did](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/17/world/europe/peter-thiel-rome-antichrist-catholics.html).

There are more than a few things Thiel says in this Verge article that make it even more obvious to me that he has very little understanding of the moral foundations of Catholic teaching.

> *“I did not come to Rome to try to be more Catholic than the pope, but I did hope, even as a Protestant, to be more Catholic than the average Catholic,” Thiel says.*

What's wild to me is that he can say something like this with so much confidence and seemingly have no idea why it's such a misguided statement. With all these lecture leaks, he seems to believe he can intellectualize his way into understanding Catholicism, while completely missing some of the very things that make Catholic teaching what it is. Catholicism isn't just an intellectual framework to make sense of history or politics. There's a moral and spiritual foundation to it that requires something more than being clever or well read. Simply using biblical language or invoking the writings of Pope Benedict XVI doesn't mean you actually understand the faith or the moral obligations that come with it.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162414)

Read this [article too](https://firstthings.com/the-pope-and-the-antichrist/), apprently it was written back in July 15, 2026, must've missed this when it came out.

> Benedict believed he was living in the end times. This claim shocks us, because Benedict chose not to speak openly on this topic until the final years of his life, at which point he had resigned the papacy, his allies had been purged from Vatican leadership, and almost nobody was listening.

Thiel looks at [Joseph Ratzinger's](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GeOcKHxQ5qI) study of apocalyptic theology as evidence of a personal apocalyptic conviction, but ignores his take on the dictatorship of relativism, he takes remarks about the Antichrist as proof that Pope Benedict believed the final crisis was already underway, and even interprets his resignation as some kind of coded sign. It reveals how much he's willing to interpret through his own worldview.

Thiel moves back and forth between completely different meanings of the Antichrist. Sometimes he's talking about a literal figure at the end of history, other times a spiritual or even political force, a cultural movement, or simply someone whose ideas he finds dangerous.

Take Marc Andreessen, for example:

> *“It’s not Andreessen, by the way. I think Andreessen is not the Antichrist. Because, you know, the Antichrist is popular.”*

But those meanings aren't interchangeable. You can't move between theological doctrine, political speculation, and personal judgments about people as if they're all describing the same thing. At some point, you're no longer interpreting scripture.

And I think that's ultimately what bothers me about all of this. The irony is that Thiel seems so convinced he understands something that he might be missing the very thing he's trying to understand.

Also his conjecture based on piecemeal research sounds a lot like bad prompting. You collect a handful of references, connect them in whatever way supports your original assumptions, and end up with an answer that sounds incredibly convincing without necessarily being true. 

I do wonder if Thiel has just tried praying instead and asking God directly for answers.

> The bond market is a fascinating place. Unlike the stock market, it can move up and down for both “good” and “bad” reasons, and those reasons can be highly subjective. That makes fixed income a wonderful financial Rorschach test.

Specific factors:

> Inflation was already uncomfortably high in many countries, and the energy disruptions from the war on Iran have worsened the problem. Inflation is the nemesis of fixed income, so it is natural that investors will demand greater yields to hold them.

2. GLOBAL GROWTH is crazy good

> The global economy has proven remarkably resilient this year, and that has forced interest rate expectations higher as well. Alphaville actually has [some sympathy](https://ftav.substack.com/p/is-stephen-miran-right) with the global growth argument,

uh-hu... break-even rates are more or less flat, meaning it *cannot be* a generalized debasement trade/everyone rushing out of bonds for fear of inflation

items.title: Why STRC (Stretch) Can't Keep Par: WTF is Digital Credit, Anyway? (Eric Yakes)
items.text:
Ah, back to *this* topic: *From hating on one type of financialized crap (=loyalty programs) to another (financialized bitcoin; shitcoin companies)*

## MONEY DOESN'T HAVE A CAPITAL STRUCTURE;

![](https://m.stacker.news/162351)

> there is a fundamental issue with STRC existing as anything but a stablecoin. I believe this is true for pure-play publicly traded bitcoin treasury companies in general and they may never “hold par” for this reason. I actually don’t believe such a structure should ever hold par regardless, but the best version of it is a stablecoin, and it needs to exist at scale in a competitive environment to function.

Fits well into the "par price of money" we're thinking about these post-Mehrling days (https://stacker.news/items/1595092, https://stacker.news/items/1596093, https://stacker.news/items/1428602)

DIGITAL CAPITAL:

> When Michael Saylor calls STRC digital capital, credit, money, or any of these vague terms, he means that **converting Bitcoin’s capital appreciation into a fixed payment is needed to make it closer to money today. Put simply, trade the upside for downside protection, and you get stability.**

That must be the most succinct, non-judgy, two-sentence description of what these (surviving... https://stacker.news/items/1521292 let's be honest, most of them are dead/dying https://stacker.news/items/1519091) treasury companies are up to.

> if bitcoin goes up a lot, then a financial structure that trades away the upside to limit the downside creates the stability needed to use it as dependable money today in a fiat economy. What is novel here is that you’re basically describing a money market fund fully backed by bitcoin. In other words, over-reserving a dollar liability by multiples in bitcoin should be able to reliably keep a peg to the US dollar and pay interest.

Waaait, waiiit. Didn't we try this once...

## The Conflict of Interests in the Capital Structure

> Strategy is a company with a capital structure, and because of that, it is criticized for the conflicts of interest that come from it. [Parker Lewis has been publicly critical](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mhFZxgauWPQ) of treasury companies for reasons that, in my opinion, are primarily related to this. My pushback on these criticisms is that, yes, there are conflicts of interest between equity holders, preferred equity holders, and other tranches of capital…but every capital structure has conflicts of interest. That is the fundamental nature of a capital structure.

> This is simply the nature of a company. **Money —is not a company. Money is a commodity** for the vast expanse of history. In recent years, in the fiat economy, it is a debt contract, and that contract needs to be homogeneous. It must remain homogeneous to be fungible.

THIIIIS:

> When you take a slice of a capital structure and call it money, it must be independent of other liabilities. **Being a slice of a capital structure means that it, at any point, can have a senior or subordinate claim issued, which will have the “issuer,” in this case management (ie, Saylor) forced to choose** between making a decision that supports either the “money” sleave or the equity sleave or the senior convertible credit or anything else at all.

Exactly. We've seen that in the last twelve-ish months: Saylor picked management/insiders/benefactors and (one of) the preferred equities... by sacrificing some bitcoin *but* *mostly* diluting commons like crazy. Owners of MSTR have been insanely diluted (SHAFTED! SCALPED!), no matter the accounting tricks they've employed to hide it and the talking points they've distributed to the sycophantic podcasters. (https://stacker.news/items/1513175, https://stacker.news/items/1292636). **Have fun staying poor, bagholder suckers.**

## "This is the problem with something like STRC being “money” or money-like. It’s part of a capital structure, which inevitably distorts its value and, thus, its fungibility."

It's difficult to account for/properly assess an interest-bearing monetary token (1/365th of the annual interest, added back to the banknote every day??). Deposit accounts at major commercial banks *sort of* abstract away from that -- by paying you *some* interest on your balance, but *mostly* just bag the convenience yield and/or customer inattention (https://stacker.news/items/1598123).

## "A stablecoin is the purest version of fiat economics. The government issues debt, debt backs the money, and nobody is in between."

Interesting observation... All those who came to bitcoin to "be your own bank" or exit the banking system will find a new home:

> The stablecoin architecture completely disintermediates the banking system and domestic banking institutions **will fight it until the bitter end for this reason. Banks exist because regulations allow them to, not competition.** https://stacker.news/items/1598910
> Stablecoins can and should be able to pay interest. Debt pays interests, debt backs currency, and the stablecoin layer blends the heterogenous debt contracts into a single homogenous token that is fungible. This is obviously what every consumer wants. A dollar asset that pays them interest. Because of their efficiency, stablecoins can pay much more.

Aaaaaaand, TL;DR, **stablecoins will always beat out Saylornomics**

> I don’t expect STRC economics (overcollateralized bitcoin) to be how this starts. I think fiat-backed stablecoins with large bitcoin reserves that allow them to pay more interest than any other pure fiat reserve issuer is how it emerges.

...screw u, Blok.

> The optimal stablecoin is a dollar-pegged, interest-paying offshore stablecoin that is backed by actual bitcoin and is redeemable in bitcoin. I think that is the end state, and it is starting with 5% of the reserve in Tether.

items.title: Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash: SoV -> transactional UoA -> MoE -> Global UoA
items.text:
When evaluating the progress of the Bitcoin protocol over the past 17 years, we can observe its undeniable success as a decentralized store of value. Within our community, we frequently rely on the historical analogy of hard money: just as gold replaced primitive monies like salt or glass beads due to its superior capacity to store value and be minted into units, we assume a mathematically scarcer asset will inevitably replace the US Dollar.

This assumption underestimates the incumbent fiat architecture. The US Dollar is not salt; it is a highly sophisticated network that successfully replaced 5,000 years of gold dominance. The Federal Reserve does not operate blindly; they engineer inflation at a measured, deliberate pace—extracting wealth slowly enough over decades to maintain the currency's network effect without triggering a sudden, collective rejection by the population. To compete with an architecture this entrenched, a hard money cannot simply rest on its absolute scarcity. It must compete directly at the point of human use.

**The Missing Sequence: The Transactional Unit of Account**

Our foundational assumption has often been a direct transition sequence: Store of Value (SoV) -> Medium of Exchange (MoE) -> Global Unit of Account (UoA).

Practical economics, however, dictates a necessary intermediate step: **Store of Value -> transactional Unit of Account (transactional UoA) -> Medium of Exchange -> Global Unit of Account.**

Before any asset can be effectively exchanged (MoE), the seller must price it, and the buyer must seamlessly comprehend that price (transactional UoA). If the accounting unit imposes a heavy cognitive load, the transaction faces friction. We observe this in economies experiencing severe inflation, where populations frequently default to centralized digital fiat (such as USDT) rather than sats, simply because the cognitive pricing model of the Dollar is easier to use.

**The Cognitive Friction of the Base Unit**

The protocol’s base limit of 2.1 quadrillion (2,100,000,000,000,000) sats is a brilliant engineering parameter for machine-level divisibility and long-term security. The 80,000 nodes securing this network provide a thermodynamic wall that is absolutely essential. However, for human accounting, this parameter introduces severe unit bias.

Pricing 10 gallons of fuel at 700 sats requires users to continually parse numbers that are unnecessarily large. If we wait 50 to 100 years for global fiat inflation to naturally make the sat scale user-friendly, we risk allowing the fiat system to further degrade the global economy. If sat remains strictly an SoV, our node operators are securing a pristine settlement layer, but the vision of peer-to-peer electronic cash remains unresolved.

**Proposing a Dual-Unit Architecture**

To provide a viable alternative to the incumbent fiat system within this decade, we need a transactional unit of account mathematically bound to the timechain, yet cognitively optimized for human transactions.

I propose examining the utility of ⁠nah•sovereign•diamond⁠. Its total circulating supply is 85.3 trillion. This specific parameter was designed to approximate the scale of the global M2 money supply, creating a natural cognitive bridge for users.

By utilizing nah via the Runes protocol (OP_RETURN), everyday commodities can be priced in low, whole numbers—for example, pricing that same fuel at 30 nahs rather than 700 sats. This bimetallic approach preserves the thermodynamic security of sat as the reserve settlement layer, while utilizing nah to eliminate the friction of the transactional unit of account. Both units scale symbiotically on the same timechain: sats provide the institutional settlement and routing liquidity, while nahs provide the retail pricing interface.

**Careful Trade-offs and the Path Forward**

Implementing this system requires a careful evaluation of trade-offs and current technical limitations. Validating nah currently requires running a heavy indexer that parses all unrelated OP_RETURN data across the network, demanding significant storage and memory overhead. Furthermore, it lacks integration with the Lightning Network for low-latency retail routing. We must not casually burden the existing 80,000 nodes with unoptimized state bloat.

These are engineering challenges, not protocol flaws. I propose the following collaborative efforts for the community:

1. **Develop a Pruned, Lightweight Indexer:** We need a specialized, open-source indexer (a "nah-core") designed exclusively to scan the base layer for sat and nah transactions, automatically discarding all other unrelated OP_RETURN data. This careful pruning will drastically lower the hardware barrier, allowing standard node operators to easily verify the 85.3 trillion supply without compromising their primary L1 duties.

2. **Lightning Network Integration:** We must build the necessary channels and liquidity pools to route nahs over Lightning, utilizing sats as collateral to enable instant retail transactions.

By optimizing the indexer and treating nah as the transactional unit of account, we can complete the evolution from a decentralized store of value to a true global medium of exchange. It is an engineering task worth our collective focus.

items.title: FFP is a Cartel: In Defense of Manchester City
items.text:
Perhaps the biggest controversy in soccer today is the penalization of Manchester City F.C., one of the "Big Six" clubs of English football, and the most successful over the last 15 years, for breaking Financial Fair Play (FFP) laws that govern the finances of clubs.

For some background, Manchester City wasn't a major English club until 2008, when they were acquired by the Abu Dhabi United Group, a holding firm for the Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan and the royal family of the United Arab Emirates. Prior to then, Man City had only minimal success, including a couple of English First Division titles in 1968 and 1937, and four FA Cup victories all prior to the 70s. This pales in comparison to their crosstown rivals Manchester United, as well as other English giants such as Liverpool and Arsenal, all with multiple league titles and FA Cup trophies across multiple eras, and European Champions League triumphs for the former two teams. Although not a small club, per se, City had not had consistent glory over their 128 year history, even facing the occasional relegation to the Second Division of English football. 

Beginning with the Emirati acquisition, their new ownership began spending heavily, signing world class talents like Carlos Tevez, Sergio Aguero, Kevin de Bruyne, and Erling Haaland to fill out their squad over the next two decades. The sudden rise in quality of players allowed them to compete with the prestigious legacy clubs of England, and their watershed moment came in 2012 when Aguero [scored a last minute goal](https://youtu.be/ssiKKjOMNrM)on the final day of the Premier League to catapult them above Manchester United in the rankings and the club's first league championship since 1968. Since then, they've won an additional 7 Premiere League titles, 4 FA Cups, and the European Champions League in 2023, becoming only the second English team besides Manchester United in 1999 to earn the "treble"- a league championship, cup championship, and European championship all in the same year.

But now the party might be coming to an end. English courts have found Man City guilty of inflating sponsorship revenues, hiding operating costs, misstating financial accounts, breaching spending limits, and a number of other FFP violations. Although City will likely appeal and drag out the court process, it is looking increasingly likely that they will be punished through some combination of stripped titles and trophies, financial penalties, or forced relegation.

Every bit of media coverage I've seen of this story has been harshly negative towards them, and while I completely agree that it is likely City and their parents at the Abu Dhabi United Group did in fact engage in financial hijinks to cover up their cash injections into the club, I believe this misses the broader point: FFP is itself a corrupt system, created to protect the legacy clubs of England and Europe from new blood and greater competition.

The basic idea behind Financial Fair Play is a system of financial regulations in European football designed to prevent clubs from spending excessively relative to the revenue they generate. The belief behind it is that football clubs should operate as financially sustainable businesses rather than relying on wealthy owners to cover their losses. In other words, a club that only generates, say, $70 million in revenue from tickets, merchandise, sponsorships, broadcast rights, etc., should only be allowed to spend approximately that much on player wages and other annual expenses. Wealthy owners, be they billionaires like Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich, who owned Chelsea football club for a long period, or the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia that owns Newcastle F.C., or Qatar Sports Investments that owns Paris Saint-Germain, would not be allowed to inject their own seemingly-limitless capital into the club and make it more competitive on the domestic and continental stage.

However, the real effect of FFP is that it protects legacy football clubs that have achieved tremendous success in the past, before FFP regulations were in place: Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Barcelona, Juventus, AC Milan, and Bayern Munich. Such clubs, owing to their rich history, have enormous fan bases spread across the world, leading to large revenue streams across all of the aforementioned products. This, in turn, enables them to outspend smaller clubs that don't have such large fan bases and revenue streams, and therefore cannot compete in the market to sign the best players and biggest stars. 

The way smaller clubs achieved parity with those historic giants was to become acquired by an entity such as Abu Dhabi United Group, the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, Qatar Sports Investments or Roman Abramovich, and then their deep-pocketed owners would use their own funds to make them competitive. FFP exists to create a regulatory barrier to entry for these parties under the guise of "fairness," pulling up the ladder behind the legacy football behemoths. 

Financial Fair Play is also a good example of a cartel, as described in economics: an arrangement between otherwise competing firms to restrict competition for their own benefit. In the Premier League, clubs collectively vote on rules governing their own competitive environment, creating a potential conflict of interest. This was, interestingly enough, demonstrated in a November 2025 vote by the Premier League clubs 14 to 6 in favor of a new "Squad Cost Revenue" system that ties spending to each club's individual revenue, rejecting a separate proposal that would've placed a common ceiling on spending. All six of the dissenting votes came from clubs outside of the traditional Big Six, demonstrating that these votes often align with each club's individual interests.

In Germany, there is a rule known as 50% + 1 that requires the majority of ownership for any club in the country to be by the fans themselves, never any singular entity. The premise behind this rule is to keep football clubs there community owned and controlled, outside the hands of billionaires, corporations, and sovereign wealth funds. However, what it has also done is create a monopoly by one giant club: Bayern Munich. Owing to its historical success dating back to the 70s, when they had stars such as Franz Beckenbauer and Gerd Muller, Bayern generates far more revenue and drastically outspends every other German club. The result is domination: they've won 34 of 63 Bundesliga titles since 1963, including 11 consecutive from 2013 to 2023, and 21 DFB Pokals. Although this system has its defenders, I'm of the belief that it produces a boring competition when you know the winner with 90%+ certainty from the outset. The fundamental reason to watch any sport is uncertainty about the eventual winner, and when one team can collect all of the best talent year-in, year-out, and dominate the competition, it significantly diminishes any excitement or incentive to be a fan and viewer.

In summation, FFP and similar rules like 50%+1 should be scrapped, and, instead, we should allow **more** large money interests to acquire and inject outside capital into smaller football clubs, enabling them to compete with historical giants. This produces a more exciting contest relative to seeing the usual characters, such as Bayern Munich, Real Madrid, Barcelona or Manchester United dominate.

items.title: Framing the question: what is money?
items.text:
*originally written by* [*Peag Blog*](https://twitter.com/PeagCafe) *on 2024-01-29.*
### What is money?

Everybody uses money. Cash, coins, cards, electronic. Its such a fundamental technology that we don't even tend to consider it as tech. We simply earn it, spend it, and save some if we can.

Most of us don't ever stop to think about what money is. That is, not it until it breaks, until the debit card is empty, or inflation destroys purchasing power. Then we scramble, trying to understand what just happened. We may jump to blaming foreigners, ideological opponents, or the other political party, when in reality is simply that our money is broken.

So, what *is* money?

Money is one of humanity's oldest social technologies, so fundamental to our lives that it can be hard to see---kind-of like asking a fish to describe water. But, look closely: money is a tool for doing, a mirror of our treasuring, a measure to talk about value, and a way to coordinate human action.

### a tool for doing | heart

Our hearts purpose to do things. Money is often a tool we use to do whatever we've decided to do. The vast majority of us, even when cooking dinner at home, paid for the groceries with money. When you need new clothes, do you make them or buy them? What about your kids' education? Whether you buy books for school or homeschool supplies, pay college tuition, or hire a private tutor, you probably use money to give your kids an education.

We use money to secure what we need as individuals and families: food, shelter, health-care, education, entertainment, communications. Money serves as a tool we use to accomplish what we've decided to do.

### a mirror of our treasuring | soul

However, money is more than just a useful tool. It often becomes an object of treasure, the thing we desire, or we use it to buy the things we treasure. When this happens, rather than our mastering money, money masters us. Like a mirror reflecting one's image, money shows us what we treasure deep-down. Police and investigative journalists know that you will eventually find the truth if you follow the money. If you want to see what a person really loves, look at their wallet or bank account.

Think of Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge before his transformation: his stingeiness showed the depths of his cold-hearted misers' isolation. Contrast him with the magi in Matthew's gospel, who embarked on a long expensive journey to bring costly gifts to a newborn child-king. Money is a mirror that reveals what we love deep down.

### measuring value | mind

Money is our social technology for measuring value. We're all familiar with prices. But why do they change? Why is a merchant happy to sell, their customer happy to buy, and both people think they got the better deal? Because we each value things subjectively, and we use money as our common language for talking about value. The woman who buys an apple values it more than the cash she pays the seller, and the guy who grew the apple values the apple less than the cash he receives. As long as neither person is being coerced to buy or sell at a given price---i.e., if they're all transacting freely---each person gains from the transaction.

Prices communicate information. Fredrick Hayek got a Nobel Prize for explaining this. Prices signal to entrepreneurs and businesses where they can meet needs expressed through the price, and if those businesses can provide that good or service below the market price, they make money on the exchange. In this sense, money is our societal language for talking about value. While money isn't the only way to value things, it is one of the primary ways across society that we measure value.

This aspect of money is sometimes tricky for us moderns to understand. For the past century or so, most of us have lived in societies where central banks and commercial banks create money out of nothing via loans. What this has meant is that the overall quantity of monetary units has increased faster than real economic productivity, which looks like rising prices from within our economic and monetary system.

For example, a house built in the 1970s may have sold for $30,000; and the same house today may command $280,000. Assuming the house was well-maintained and the neighborhood hadn't changed much, is the house really worth more? Its still a house, providing shelter to someone in the same spot it was 50 years ago. Or has the money simply lost a whole lot of its purchasing power? If we measured the same house using ounces of gold as our monetary measure, we would probably see its price as far more stable over the long-term. Using a money where the overall quantity of money in the economy can constantly change is similar to a carpenter trying to frame a house with a tape measure that changed the length of its unit of measure each day.

### coordinating people | strength

Finally, money is a way to coordinate human action. Have you had a project to do that's bigger or more complex than your skill set or time? When the plumbing breaks, do you take time to learn plumbing yourself (some do!) or do you call a plumber and pay him to fix it? When your computer breaks, do you fiddle with it yourself or call tech support? When a large household has to move, they could do all the work themselves, or they could easily convince strangers to help them by hiring a moving company, using money to coordinate a lot of extra experienced hands for a big move.

Money can multiply one's strength and ability to coordinate people. Think of any large project people plan together, like building a house, starting a school, or running a business. In all likelihood, if more than one person is involved, one will use money to coordinate the actions of a variety of people to achieve a common goal. Even when organizing volunteers, one needs money for supplies and other costs. Often, if sufficient funding isn't the, the project won't even get started. As Jesus of Nazareth once said, "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28), for fear of being mocked if one starts such a project without the means to finish it.

## Conclusion

Jesus point with the tower-building story was about the cost of following him as a disciple. How we understand and use money has direct bearing on how, if Christian, one follows Jesus. We've seen that money is a tool for purposeful doing, a mirror of our treasuring, a measure to talk about value, and a way to coordinate human action. Those categories all touch on discipleship, the way Christians walk with Jesus.

Jesus evoked those four categories of human action when he answered a question regarding the most important of God's commandments, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these." (Mark 10:29-31)

Money touches our hearts' purposes, our soul's treasure, our mind's economic calculations, and the strength in which we can coordination others actions with our ends. One's understanding of money provides endless opportunities to walk as disciples of Jesus.

May the Lord give you wisdom in your use of money, that heart, soul, mind, and strength you would use this tool to display love for God and for your neighbor.

items.title: Is Bitcoin already freedom money?
items.text:
While at TABConf, I had a couple of interesting conversations with [Wizardsardine](https://wizardsardine.com/) cofounder Kevin Loaec. He seemed to be feeling that Bitcoin is in a holding pattern of sorts and that it is not likely to change very much in the near future.

A few days ago, I saw that he posted these observations:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162333)

[source](https://x.com/KLoaec/status/2111481140305666300)

He goes on to observe that most of the world doesn't see Bitcoin this way. Normies seem to think it's a scam or a get-rich-quick scheme and don't associate it with freedom at all (I would add that normies don't seem to think the financial system they use poses any threat to their freedom at all). 

Loaec said he is content with Bitcoin, which is something I hear many Bitcoiners say:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162338)

[source](https://x.com/KLoaec/status/2111481144159916307)

But then he asked a question which I found interesting:

> # The question is: can we make people understand Bitcoin is freedom money, or are we only building for ourselves?

Most of the people I spoke with at TABConf felt that Bitcoin adoption wasn't going to increase any time soon. Nobody (other than @real_paul_sztorc?) was pushing for one last fork that will bring the crowds running. Most of the business-owners I spoke with were hoping to find customers among the group of people who are already Bitcoiners. Bringing in the normies was not on the table.

If Bitcoin is already freedom money (which to me means that I can retreat to bitcoin if the traditional financial system decided to eject/debank/censor me, and that I can hold my savings in bitcoin without being wrecked by inflation), perhaps the answer to Loaec's question is yes, at this point we are building for ourselves.

However, there are two points to consider here:

1. If Bitcoin is freedom money, adoption will occur when people need freedom, which is to say, when financial repression or taxation or inflation increase. Perhaps Bitcoiners should be advocating for governments to implement more repressive financial policies. 

2. I did not immediately agree with Loaec that Bitcoin is already freedom money. Holding bitcoin is fine. Spending it is still difficult. I'm not convinced that Bitcoin is at the state where it preserves my freedom should the traditional financial system decide to shut me out. 

# Do you think Bitcoin already serves as freedom money?

items.title: Here’s the Truth About Fertility (Critic Mag, Stephen Shaw)
items.text:
Meant to write about this the other week but alas not... and today is the day:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162280)

The author, Stephen Shaw, even has a (peer-reviewed!!) article in *Nature* on the phenomenon with the non-catchy title "[On a microdemographic framework for decomposing contemporary fertility dynamics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-11522-9)".

## "We don’t get to choose to become parents. We get to *hope* to become one."

> from the data that hope is far more fragile than we might like to admit. Yet we have built our lives around the assumption that becoming a parent remains largely within our control, right up to some mythical cliff around the age of 35. Therein lies the untruth at the heart of the debate around fertility which has been raging

I got recommended *Birthgap*, the documentary that Shaw spent the last decade or so making, and found it extraordinary and captivating. It's two bloody hours, but I watched it all in one dinner/post-dinner sitting.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m2GeVG0XYTc

*Warning:* I never felt more blackpilled than after that. Hopeless etc.

> Earlier this year, the UN published a [flagship report](https://www.unfpa.org/publications/lives-choices-and-futures-demographic-futures-survey) covering more than 70 nations, rich and poor alike. It found that among childless 35 to 39-year-olds, over 70 per cent of women still want children. For men it is even higher, at almost 80 per cent.
> That follows a report titled [The Real Fertility Crisis](https://www.unfpa.org/swp2025), published by the UN in 2025, again spanning richer and poorer nations. It concluded that **millions of people are unable to have the number of children they want.**

But it's not family size or the *number of kids* a mother has... it's the *number of people who become parents!* **Childlessness is the disease.**

> Through decades of increasing educational and career opportunities for women, the ups and downs of economic cycles, and enormous shifts in cultural norms, from Japan to the UK to the US, mothers have been having around the same number of children as prior recent generations. But instead of a trend to smaller families, childlessness since the 1970s has rocketed.

Also, it's not true that the feminist lady boss (who thinks promiscuous sex is a ~~god~~darwin-given right and *never* wants to rent out her womb to the patriarchy...) is everywhere:

> And only a small minority, **ranging from around 4 to 14 per cent and averaging about 7 per cent**, said their ideal was no children at all, lower than most of us have come to believe given the headlines in the media these days.

## "If today’s fertility patterns hold, nearly 40 per cent of women in these nations will remain childless for life, against just 7 per cent who say that is what they want."

*Explanations?* The pill, screens, (relative) poverty, housing market?

Nope, **just a broken societal/matching-up culture:**

> The strongest explanation I have found, though I would stop short of calling it proven, is what researchers call pair-bonding: finding the right person, settling down and, often but not always, getting married.

> Model that across a population and the pattern appears. As parenthood is pushed later, the odds that two people will find each other and commit fall in a predictable curve, just like the one we find across all 40 nations in my research, without exception. More time to find a match produces more single people, and consequently fewer parents.
> Two people can each be doing everything “right,” genuinely want a family, and still miss each other, because success now depends on someone else’s timing too, not just your own. That makes it hard to point the finger at childless people, as Perrins does, and say they simply didn’t want it enough.

**Incredible:**

![](https://m.stacker.news/162282)

***

Here the take-away in [Twitter form](https://x.com/StephenJShaw/status/2101783634466451669):

https://x.com/StephenJShaw/status/2101783634466451669

## "trying hard enough barely comes into it. Finding your match is personal. Matching is a societal phenomenon. And societies that delay parenthood aren't helping themselves."

> \[Children-per-Mother] has been remarkably stable (mothers aren’t having dramatically fewer kids once they start), while \[Total-Maternal Rate] has shown sharp, shock-like drops (more women simply never becoming mothers).

items.title: Nostr4j v0.4.1 : unstoppable p2p etc...
items.text:
[Nostr4j](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/) is a cross-platform Java library that handles most Nostr protocol details for you, with security, strong typing, and efficiency built into its design. Alongside hardening and careful memory management, it caches and reuses data to avoid unnecessary conversions and allocations. 

*The same code compiles for Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, and browsers through JavaScript or WebAssembly.*

**The newly released version 0.4.1** comes with a new website with the full documentation and live examples: [https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/) , and with a lot of fixes and improvements, including:

# Improved P2P networking

Nostr4j has a built-in **p2p networking stack (aka** [**NIP-DC**](https://github.com/NostrGameEngine/nostr4j/blob/master/NIP-DC.md)**).** This is a special (and fairly complex) protocol designed for nostr4j, that lets users coordinate on Nostr relays and then move to direct and reliable p2p connections for encrypted data exchange.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162319)

## Multi-hop routing and mesh networking

When two users can't connect directly, [multi-hop routing](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/onion-routing.html) lets their messages travel through others, forming a mesh network that users can join with at least a single connection to an existing member. Routing happens automatically, and onion encryption keeps private messages encrypted end to end, so forwarding peers can't read them.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162318)

## Distributed broadcasting

The same idea extends to broadcasting: calling `broadcast()` instead of `send()` shares delivery across users, who automatically forward messages to their neighbors.

## TURN and connection recovery

Even users on networks that block direct P2P can join through a blind [WebSocket relay](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/turn-server.html), which forwards encrypted binary data it can't read. These users can participate in multi-hop routing and bridge isolated groups.

The [P2P stack](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/p2p-overview.html) mixes and matches all available paths and switches to more direct connections as they become available.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162321)

## Simple p2p streams

Nostr4j now offers a simple abstraction over a subset of its P2P stack, built on standard Java input and output streams, so apps can use it just like regular Java I/O without handling any networking details.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162322)

# Local event caching

Beyond networking, the release adds more options for [local event caching](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/event-cache.html). You can keep events in memory, persist them through a virtual filesystem, or supply your own [event store](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/event-stores.html). `NostrCacheRelay` then exposes those events to your `NostrPool` as a regular relay, so you query cached data the same way as you would do for online relays.

# Relay pool management

Managing large relay lists is also easier with [connection budgets, priorities, and hints](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/relay-hints.html). Your app can adjust priorities as its needs change, and Nostr4j keeps the relevant relays connected without opening the entire list at once. Hints give priority to relays likely to hold the events you're fetching or subscribing to, for as long as the operation is active. Meanwhile, a [background queue](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/progressive-publication.html) makes a best-effort attempt to deliver events to every inactive registered relay.

![](https://m.stacker.news/162323)

# More

* [NIP-42 authentication](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/nip-42.html) for relays that require it.
* [NIP-59 gift wrapping](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/nip-59.html) for private messages.
* [WebLN support](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/webln.html) and [QR pairing for compatible Nostr Wallet Connect wallets](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/wallets.html#let-the-user-pair-through-a-qr-code).
* [Extended Blossom support](https://ngengine.org/nostr4j/docs/blossom.html), with mirroring and  media optimization
* ln address support in nwc pairing url

—

I built this mainly for my own projects, but I hope others will find it useful too.

items.title: Capitalist UBI via AI, and What Even is a Dividend? (Matt Levine, Money Stuff)
items.text:
## The way we distribute economic value today is **inside** and **outside** of a corporate structure.

**Inside**, you have a firm trying to assemble resources (labor, land, tech, capital) in ways that enhance value for consumers. They pay market-determined expenses to these factors of production (wages, rent, interest), and the proof in the pudding is whether or not they have something left over *after* those expenses are done.

From the left-over funds, the corporation sends 21% to "society," proxied by a benevolent wonderful government here to help and assist us all; and the 79% gets sent to shareholders (who *also*, strangely, fork over a bunch to "society" for the privilege of receiving their corporation's final value-add).

At every level here, there's some accounting tricks and dillydallying (subsidies; pay management above-market wages to move surplus from the outside pot to the inside pot; give employees company cars and perks; throw massive company party twice a year *provided* those expenses are tax deductible), but that's roughly the idea:

![](https://m.stacker.news/162382)

> At some companies, **most of the economic value goes to the founder; at others, to outside institutional shareholders.** You could tell various stories about why that might make sense: Maybe some companies were bootstrapped and owe all of their success to their founders’ efforts, so the founders keep most of the value; other companies grew over time by deploying lots of outside capital and are run by hired professional managers, so the investors get most of the value. Or maybe it’s like “this company raised money from shareholders when valuations were high and terms were founder-friendly, so the founders kept most of the value.”

**Now, imagine AI takes over everything in the benevolent version.**

There's almost no labor income left, so you can't tax that... maybe society gets its cut through annual service fees/poll tax sort of arrangements, city-state style, or maybe some property taxes, or maybe the corporate profits are waaay higher now that there aren't any wages to pay in the *inside* portion. Anyway, there's some value distributed back to society over and above the market-based compensation of factors -- again, we're assuming benevolent, nice governments here, just looking out for your wellbeing.

* So, **Anthropic** said they'll make a PUBLIC BENEFIT FUND of 5% of its shares (with extra allocations later on as/when the company gets more valuable) *plus* it wants the prerogative to decide how to spend the gains "towards the public good"/mitigating AI labor market impacts etc. *Very nice, very sweet.*
* And then Mr. **Muskman of SpaceX** said: naah, I'll just give shares to every kid in America (works out to about 0.5% of his holdings). Distribute the ownership (https://stacker.news/items/1279014, https://stacker.news/items/1438025) and assets, and people can choose for themselves how to spend the "public" good. *Very individualist/direct.*

## "I guess those are the three possibilities? Give 5% (or 0.5%) of your stock to the government, or pro rata to everyone (or every child), or to a nonprofit foundation that tries to do what is best for society."

EXCELLENT and wonderfully symbolic summary:

> Each AI lab’s proposal is pleasingly characteristic: OpenAI wants to work with the government, SpaceX is libertarian and individualistic and cost-conscious, \[3]  and Anthropic wants to make the decisions about what is best for society. **Competing visions about how to build AI, and also competing visions about how to give society its cut.**

***

## Also: DIVIDENDS as income

> Arguably *the main condition of human flourishing is passive income.*
> Realistically, though, most people can’t live on passive income. Somebody has to make all the stuff that the leisurely aristocrats consume. It takes quite a lot of capital to live on passive income. Traditionally, if you wanted $100,000 a year of passive income, that would require between $2 million and $2.5 million of capital.

## "It’s hard to accumulate that much capital, and so a basic goal of finance is to create higher-yielding forms of passive income"

*Where does the yield come from* is preceded by *financial engineering **generating** said yield*

**stage 1**: agriculture... not very high yielding, limited to what the land could produce
**stage 2**: gov bonds, VOC/EIC, British consols, war bonds: higher yield (4%-ish in the heyday of the British Empire) -- very safe, usually... sometimes goes to shit https://stacker.news/items/1599101
**Stage 3** corporate, say 19th C railroad dividends of 7%, or 21st C Google century bonds (of 6.5% https://stacker.news/items/1430666, https://stacker.news/items/1430666) 
**Stage 4:** perpetual equities, treasury companies, options strategies and all manner of financial shenanigans! 12%, 15%, or *58%!!*

*...*and you can extend this logic further... the longer out you go risk-wise, the higher % "dividend" you can attain -- and the less capital you need to finance your amazing ["Very comfortable life"](https://x.com/saylor/status/2038646796805632330)

> In 2021 and 2022, there was a hard-to-explain-now vogue for high-yielding crypto projects sometimes referred to as Ponzicoins; we once talked about one that advertised a yield of 83,687.5%. \[...] You can get $100,000 a year in passive income with capital of just $172,500, if your capital yields 58%, so this really does fill a certain need.
> “Dividend nomads.” I feel like there’s a traditional idea of dividends where a company produces economic value and gives some of it to shareholders as a dividend. But **the category of “dividend” is capacious, and you can put arbitrarily risky gambles into a corporate form and distribute the winnings as dividends.**

Also, *don't tell Saylor!!* https://stacker.news/items/1598937 https://stacker.news/items/1457137

> Obviously the final stage of all of this is in the previous section: *Give everyone a stake in the AI companies*, produce limitless abundance via AI, and let everyone live in leisure off the AI dividends.

***
